title: United States–Korea Strategic Energy & Industrial Partnership
subtitle: Where deeper industrial integration creates strategic value, through which instruments, and where to stay out
label: Generated from Allied Industrial Base Explorer data and a curated external evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-06); evidence, sources and caveats in the appendix. Data as of 30 October 2026.
disclosure: Rule-generated from the data (R/partnerships) with external facts from a dated, curated evidence layer; not yet checked by an independent verifier. Items marked partial or unverified must be confirmed before citation.

inlines.v: Battery Materials & Cells: Natural graphite (joint); Battery recycling feed (US->Korea); Accumulator parts & separators (Korea->US). Nuclear Fuel & Reactor Systems: Nuclear extraction (joint). Permanent Magnets & Drive Systems: Rare-earth oxides & compounds (US->Korea); Rare-earth permanent magnets (joint); AC generators (US->Korea). Grid Equipment & Conductors: Copper smelting & refining (joint). Solar Manufacturing: Polysilicon (US->Korea).

Recognise trusted partner supply of electric vehicles refining (rare-earth metals, rare-earth oxides & compounds); rare-earth oxides & compounds; accumulator parts & separators in procurement and content rules. Common anti-circumvention rules for rare-earth permanent magnets. Bind market access for wind components (ac generators, ferrite & other magnets, insulators & bushings). Keep uranium/fuel extraction: aggregated low-coverage sub-sectors (spent fuel & nuclear scrap, uranium ores); nuclear special materials; transformers open to global sourcing.
Upgrade US-Korea Strategic Investment MOU and Special Act (US$350bn): sector strategy, reciprocal commitments, a KPI dashboard and an annual review. No new MOU.

Do not co-subsidise new Electric Vehicles components (accumulator parts & separators, electric motors, ferrite & other magnets) capacity. Do not co-subsidise new Batteries assembly (li-ion cells & packs, other accumulators) capacity. Do not co-subsidise new Electric Vehicles assembly (electric & plug-in cars, electric buses, trucks & tractors, electric two-wheelers & works trucks) capacity.

Of 142 technology x stage cells and electro-industrial nodes assessed for the pair, 39 show an active complementarity (a supplier meeting the other's need, a shared chokepoint, a capacity-constrained trusted supplier or a chain specialisation), 3 direct competition and 74 no strategic case. The relationship is not one of general similarity: most of the electro-industrial base needs no bilateral intervention.

AIB strategic roles: US Demand & Market Anchor (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (primary), Capital & Investment Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (secondary), Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (secondary); Korea Specialized Technology & Manufacturing Anchor (primary), Scale Manufacturing & Integration Platform (primary), Coordination / Bridge Hub (secondary), Capital & Investment Anchor (secondary).

Korea supplies accumulator parts & separators, solar cells, cathode materials & precursors, gallium, germanium & indium where the US is short; the US supplies polysilicon, rare-earth oxides & compounds, battery recycling feed, ac generators where Korea is short; the two share exposure to the same coercive supplier in natural graphite, rare-earth permanent magnets, copper smelting & refining, where neither can supply the other and the answer is joint demand, finance and third-country capacity.

From the AIB roles, the US brings demand and offtake, coordination across allied chains, capital; Korea brings specialised technology and manufacturing, scale manufacturing, coordination across allied chains. Public finance runs through DOE LPO, DoW OSC, DFC, EXIM on the US side and KEXIM, K-SURE, KOMIR, KDB on the Korea side. The trade is market access and demand certainty for trusted capacity.

Do not co-subsidise new Electric Vehicles components (accumulator parts & separators, electric motors, ferrite & other magnets) capacity: both are strong suppliers (US 7%, Korea 2%). Trusted supply is adequate: this is commercial competition.

Do not co-subsidise new Batteries assembly (li-ion cells & packs, other accumulators) capacity: both are strong suppliers (US 5%, Korea 5%). More trusted capacity is needed, so agree who specialises in what rather than racing.

Do not co-subsidise new Electric Vehicles assembly (electric & plug-in cars, electric buses, trucks & tractors, electric two-wheelers & works trucks) capacity: both are strong suppliers (US 8%, Korea 4%). Trusted supply is adequate: this is commercial competition.
Existing mechanisms and the MEA question
. Gaps: no cross-sector KPI dashboard or review cycle; no bilateral mechanism covers SC-BATTERIES, SC-MAGNETS, SC-GRID.
Do not sign a new energy MOU. Give USKR-M2 a sector strategy, reciprocal commitments and a KPI dashboard covering the recommended compacts, reviewed every 12 months.

This section sets out what already exists before anything new is proposed. Facts are from the curated evidence layer (accessed 2026-11-06); items marked partial or unverified rest on secondary sources and should be confirmed before citation.
Korea's memberships in OSI's economic-security agreements table: IPEF, MSP, U.S. FTA.
Senior officials meeting in New York agreed to enhance dialogue on critical minerals and cooperation in Southeast Asia and Sub-Saharan Africa through the trilateral Early Warning System.

Fact sheet states US support for a process toward Korean civil enrichment and reprocessing, subject to the 123 Agreement and US law, and approves nuclear-powered submarines; formal talks reportedly began June 2026 and were still discussing 123 revision in September 2026; no revision signed.
ASPI lists the MSP, which Korea chairs in 2025, among the frameworks for Australia-Korea minerals cooperation; Australian membership is not stated in that article.
The US-hosted ministerial in Feb 2026 was attended by Japan and Korea among others, and Korea was reported to chair the FORGE critical-minerals forum through June 2026.

Korea chaired the Minerals Security Partnership until June 2026; a February 2026 report says its 17 members carried into the successor FORGE; Korean public lenders joined the MSP Finance Network; no signed US-Korea critical-minerals MOU was found.
In the OSI energy basket, US imported US$41.2bn from Korea and Korea imported US$33.1bn from US (bilateral flows 2024, summed over the technology x stage cells).

KORUS has been in force since March 2012; amended in 2018 on autos, light trucks and investment rules without congressional action; the countries still use its consultative mechanisms; exact day of entry into force not stated in the source.

Westinghouse, KEPCO and KHNP settled their APR1400 intellectual-property dispute on 16 Jan 2025, dismissing all legal actions and setting up future cooperation on projects worldwide; terms are confidential, so market-allocation reports cannot be confirmed.

ICE detained 475 people at the US$4.3bn Georgia plant in September 2025, many Korean technicians on visa issues; Hyundai said opening slipped two to three months and reports in April 2026 said it was ready to open.

A January 2026 Section 301 petition targets Korea's treatment of Coupang, on which USTR has not acted; a July 2026 House Judiciary interim report called it discriminatory; the US also criticises the pace of Korean investment; reported January 2026 threat of 25% tariffs not in this source.

The three leaders agreed to pilot an early warning system exchanging supply-chain information via embassies in selected countries, with critical minerals and rechargeable batteries as priority products, plus an annual commerce and industry ministers track; the system is not published as operating beyond the pilot.

Sets a 15% US tariff on Korean goods (higher of KORUS, MFN or 15%), 15% Section 232 on autos and parts, no more than 15% on pharma, semiconductors no less favourable than comparable partners; commits US$350bn (US$200bn plus US$150bn shipbuilding) with a US$20bn annual cap; reproduced text, not the whitehouse.gov page.

Lutnick and Minister Kim signed the MOU on the US$200bn strategic-investment tranche, capped at US$20bn a year; reported profit split is 50:50 until principal and interest are repaid, then 10:90 in the US favour.
Investment vehicle, project pipeline and financing

The US$150bn shipbuilding half of the pledge is to be financed through direct investment, guarantees and loans led by Korean policy-finance institutions; reports say Hanwha Philly Shipyard expansion is delayed because the fund has not taken concrete shape; article date not shown.

Joint statement of 1 Oct 2026 formalises three projects: Encinal, Texas 6.3 GW gas plant (US$22.3bn), Alaska LNG (over US$50bn expected, subject to commercial reasonableness) and nuclear (up to US$120bn); the annual cap and vehicle structure are not addressed in this article.

Up to US$120bn for eight US reactors (US$100bn construction, US$20bn contingency), with a US$10bn advance payment for long-lead items targeted by year-end 2026; links to the May 2025 goal of 10 large reactors under construction by 2030; reactor designs not specified in this article.

Korean companies will pursue a significant minority stake in Westinghouse to share gains from large-reactor projects, with terms to be set in commercial talks; other reports put it at 5 to 10 percent but that figure is not in this source.
Corporate relationships in the recommended compacts
LGES agreed to supply Toyota's North American EVs with about 20 GWh a year of modules from 2025, with roughly 4 trillion won (about 3 billion dollars) invested in Michigan lines dedicated to Toyota.
SK On signed a conditional offtake with US graphite developer Westwater for battery-grade natural graphite in North America.

Multi-metal smelter project of about US$7.4bn through Crucible JV, with the Department of War reported as largest shareholder at 40% (US$760m in one account, US$1.4bn conditional in another) and a US$210m Commerce grant.

The 2023 Honda-LGES joint venture L-H Battery keeps operating its Ohio cell plant under a lease after LGES sold the building to Honda for about 4.22 trillion won (2.85 billion dollars) announced Dec 2025; a later report of a lower closing value of 3.74 trillion won is unconfirmed.
LGES agreed to sell the Ohio JV factory building and related assets to Honda for about $2.85B with the JV continuing via lease and closing targeted for 2026-02-28.

A US$200m JV, run by POSCO International as largest shareholder with ReElement refining technology, plans US NdPr-Dy-Tb oxides then magnets and motor cores, following a September 2025 MOU; no MP Materials link found.

Qcells began cell manufacturing at Cartersville, Georgia; by Q3 2026 it expects 3.3 GW each of ingot, wafer and cell and 3.5 GW of modules there, plus 5.1 GW modules at Dalton; ingot and wafer status not stated; investment not disclosed; a secondary report cites US$675m of 2026 AMPC.

Final investment decision in May 2026 after an Australian offtake commitment under the Strategic Reserve; construction began 8 Oct 2026; credit agencies from the US, Canada, Korea and Germany support it; the article's A$1.2bn figure is ambiguous.

LGES began mass production of LFP storage cells by repurposing part of its Holland, Michigan EV plant, targeting over 30 GWh by end-2026; a US$1.6bn LFP supply deal with DTE Energy is reported; publication date approximate.

Samsung SDI secured a KRW 1.5tn (about US$1bn) US ESS cell supply deal, starting with NCA before LFP; its Kokomo, Indiana line was reported starting ESS output in 2026; the StarPlus (Stellantis) and BlueOval SK joint ventures were not covered; date approximate.

Second Montgomery, Alabama plant (312,000 sq ft, about US$200m) due for completion in April and to lift extra-high-voltage transformer capacity about 50%, up to 765 kV; completion year inferred; other outlets give US$273.7m across Ulsan and Alabama.

Hyosung is investing about US$300m in a three-phase expansion of its ultra-high-voltage transformer plant in Memphis, Tennessee, and formed a JV with Quanta Services in June 2026 for extra-high-voltage circuit breakers; completion dates not given.
LS Electric plans US$240m of US investment by 2030, expanding its Utah switchgear plant and developing a Bastrop, Texas campus.
Unverified items are left out of this section; they stay in the evidence register (evidence_register.csv) and the evidence layer.

Working channels today: US-Korea Strategic Investment MOU and Special Act (US$350bn) (a project pipeline and finance); Minerals Security Partnership and FORGE (finance). What the relationship lacks: no cross-sector KPI dashboard or review cycle; no bilateral mechanism covers SC-BATTERIES, SC-MAGNETS, SC-GRID.

Korean autos and parts face a 15% Section 232 rate (combined with MFN) under the November 2025 deal, applied retroactively to 1 Nov 2025 for autos per implementing guidance; Section 232 is unaffected by the IEEPA ruling.

The deal caps future Section 232 chip tariffs for Korea, subject to talks; trade press reports a January 2026 25% Section 232 tariff on certain advanced chips with Korean memory exports to data centres largely exempt.

After the Supreme Court ruling the President lifted the EO 14257 tariffs, including Korea's 15% country rate, on 20 Feb 2026 and imposed a temporary 10% global tariff under Section 122, which expired in July 2026; refund treatment not covered.

On 23 Jul 2026 the US imposed a 12.5% tariff on most Korean goods after a Section 301 forced-labor investigation; a separate excess-capacity Section 301 probe could add tariffs and Seoul wants assurance the total stays within the agreed 15%.

Proclamation of 6 Aug 2026 sets a 15% tariff on certain derivatives and minimum import prices on polysilicon and derivatives from 4 Dec 2026; Korea's combined rate is capped at 15% under the deal; dates and scope taken from secondary summaries.
Tariffs on most Korean steel and aluminium imports remain at 50%; the fact sheet does not address them and the earlier steel quota was terminated in 2025.
